# Orb Reactor - After Effects CEP panel

A ground-up After Effects port of your "Liquid Orb Editor" web app: the same
shader-driven glass/fluid orb, all 13 presets, the idle/"thinking" state model
— now living inside a CEP panel that renders straight onto your timeline at
the current time indicator (CTI), and can react to a voice track the way
Siri's orb reacts to speech.

## What changed since the last build

- **Particle Ribbon export looked over-contrasty / different glow than
  preview.** Found it: the particle brightness/size shader math scaled
  itself against the *absolute pixel resolution* of whatever it was
  rendering to (a leftover from the original app), so a 512px preview and a
  1920px export produced visibly different-looking particles even with
  identical settings. Particle appearance is now completely decoupled from
  output resolution - preview and export always match.
- **"Use selected timeline layer" ignored the layer's trim.** It was
  analyzing and exporting against the *entire underlying audio file*,
  regardless of how the layer was trimmed on the timeline. It now reads the
  layer's actual in/out points and only considers that exact range - both
  for the reactive analysis and for "match audio length" export duration.
- **UI pass**: icons on tabs and buttons, shorter labels throughout, a
  Cancel button that appears mid-export (stops rendering immediately, kills
  ffmpeg right away for H.264, and fully resets the export section so you
  can export again immediately), the export button is just "Export" now,
  and a refined, more minimal dark theme.

- **ffmpeg is no longer bundled.** Download ffmpeg yourself and paste the
  path to the executable in Settings. The path is remembered in
  `Documents/OrbReactor/ffmpeg-path.txt` (survives CEP cache clears).
  Without a path, H.264 MP4 is shown disabled with a hint; PNG sequence
  remains the default and works in both After Effects and Premiere Pro.
- **The panel could get permanently stuck at "connecting to After Effects…"**
  after the shader-splitting change. Root cause: the generated per-preset
  shaders had a function-ordering bug (a function was defined *after* the
  code that calls it, which GLSL doesn't allow), so the very first shader
  compile at start-up threw, and since that happens before the rest of the
  script runs, nothing after it - including the connection status - ever
  updated. All 13 preset shaders are now validated with a real GLSL compiler
  as part of building this package, not just eyeballed.
- **Particle Ribbon's exported orientation/colors didn't match what was on
  screen.** The ribbon's automatic drift-rotation and its particle color
  cycling both depend on elapsed shader time, which keeps running during
  preview but always restarted from zero on export - so by the time you
  rotated it and hit export, the automatic rotation and colors had drifted
  to a different point than what you were looking at. Export now starts
  from the exact time position the preview was showing.
- **The live preview didn't match a plain export.** By default (no
  simulation or reactivity engaged), the preview was always showing the
  dim "idle" look rather than your actual slider values, while export
  defaulted to the full look - so colors/brightness could look "wrong" in
  the export compared to what you'd been staring at. The preview now shows
  exactly your slider values by default; "Preview idle look" lets you check
  the resting/silent look on demand instead of it being the default view.
- The export button just says "Export" now.
- Added a **Cancel export** button that appears while exporting - it stops
  rendering immediately (and kills ffmpeg right away for the H.264 path
  instead of waiting for it to finish), and the export section fully resets
  afterward so you can export again immediately.

- **Load time.** The panel used to compile one giant shader containing all
  13 presets' code at once - large branchy shaders like that are slow to
  compile, and that was the main cause of the ~40s start-up. Each preset now
  has its own small, single-purpose shader (`client/shader/presets/orb-lib.
  <style>.frag`, generated by `scripts/make-shader-variants.py` via
  reachability analysis over the shared helper functions). Only the default
  preset compiles synchronously at start-up; the next two (in gallery order)
  compile right after, and the rest compile quietly in the background.
  Switching to an already-warmed preset is instant; switching to one still
  warming up in the background compiles once, on demand.
- **Particle Ribbon had no glass shell.** The WebGL2 port ran either the
  glass-shell pass *or* the particle pass, never both. The shader was
  actually designed for both to run together (its preset function
  deliberately paints nothing so the shell shows through) - fixed by running
  the shell pass first and compositing particles on top, every time.
- **Idle radius was too small to see.** Idle now sits at 85% of your radius
  slider instead of shrinking dramatically - a subtle "at rest" look rather
  than nearly invisible.
- **H.264 export could hang indefinitely.** If the configured ffmpeg path
  didn't actually run (wrong OS/architecture, stale path from testing
  elsewhere), export would silently freeze on the first frame instead of
  failing. ffmpeg detection now test-runs any candidate (bundled binary,
  common install locations, system PATH) instead of just checking that a
  file exists there, and export aborts immediately with a clear message if
  ffmpeg can't actually launch, instead of hanging.
- Voice reactivity and manual "simulate talking" no longer coexist
  confusingly - enabling reactivity hides the simulate button, since the
  Pause control already freezes reactive playback too.
- "Also brighten with loudness" is on by default and no longer shown in the
  UI (it stayed useful enough to keep, just not worth a toggle).

## What changed from the web app, and why

- **WebGPU -> WebGL2.** Your original renders with WebGPU + WGSL. CEP's
  bundled Chromium build varies release to release and commonly ships with
  WebGPU disabled or unstable, but WebGL2 has been reliable across every CEP
  version in recent After Effects. I mechanically transpiled `effect.wgsl`
  to GLSL ES 3.00 (`client/shader/orb-lib.glsl`) preserving the exact math -
  every fluid preset, the glass shell, the edge-glow bank, the palette
  ramps - so the look should match your original pixel-for-pixel (modulo the
  usual float-precision noise between GPUs).
- **Particle Ribbon is an approximation.** The original renders that preset
  with ~220,000 GPU-driven particles across up to 6 layers. That's fine for a
  live WebGPU canvas; it is not something you want to push through WebGL2 in
  a CEP panel hundreds of times in a row during an export. I ported the same
  vertex math (curve, twist, palette, breathing) but at a reduced particle
  budget (`renderer.js`, `this.uSegments` / `this.vSegments`) so exports stay
  responsive. Turn those numbers up if your machine handles it fine.
- **No manual keyframing.** Like the source app, "the animation" is the
  shader's own continuous procedural motion (driven by `time` and `speed`),
  plus the idle <-> thinking state transition. There's nothing to keyframe -
  design a look, and optionally wire it to audio.

## Features

- All 13 presets, full parameter panel with a **reset icon on every slider
  and color swatch** (snaps back to that preset's default).
- Preset gallery shows **real rendered thumbnails** of each effect (lazily
  generated after the panel finishes loading, so it doesn't slow startup).
- Play/Pause control on the live preview, independent of audio - freezes the
  exact current frame rather than continuing to animate in the background.
- Load audio either from the **selected timeline layer** (its underlying
  source file) or by **browsing a file**. Voice reactivity now uses a proper
  attack/release envelope follower: the orb sits essentially flat at
  silence and its "waves" scale continuously with how loud the speech is -
  for every preset, not just Siri/Spectrum - rather than a simple two-state
  on/off snap.
- When your audio came from **file browsing** (not already on the AE
  timeline), you can have it **placed on the timeline alongside the
  rendered orb**, both starting at the same CTI, in one step.
- Two export formats:
  - **PNG sequence** - alpha-transparent, most compatible.
  - **H.264 MP4** - raw frames are piped directly into ffmpeg (no per-frame
    PNG encoding at all), which is dramatically faster for long exports.
    H.264 has no alpha channel, so pick a background color to composite onto.
- A macOS `ffmpeg` binary ships in `bin/mac/ffmpeg` and is auto-detected; you
  can point at a different one (e.g. a Windows build) in the Voice
  Reactivity tab.
- Duration/resolution/frame rate can each independently follow the audio
  length, the comp's work area / dimensions / frame rate, or a custom value.
- The particle-ribbon shader compiles lazily (only if you actually pick that
  preset), and the export renderer is reused across exports in a session,
  instead of recompiling shaders every time - both meant to keep the panel
  feeling snappy.
- **Particle Ribbon is 3D** - a small orbit dial appears top-left of the
  preview when that preset is selected. Drag to rotate, double-click to
  reset; the same orientation carries into export.
- ffmpeg is now auto-detected from the bundled binary, common install
  locations, and your system `PATH`, re-checked fresh at export time (not
  just once at launch) - the "ffmpeg path" field fills itself in when found,
  and you only need to touch it if none of that works.
- Every slider and color swatch reliably has its reset icon on the right,
  and non-essential explanations moved into hover tooltips instead of
  permanent paragraphs, so the panel reads cleaner.


## Installing

Works in **After Effects** and **Premiere Pro** on **Windows** and **macOS**.

1. Copy this whole folder into your CEP extensions directory:
   - Windows: `C:\Program Files (x86)\Common Files\Adobe\CEP\extensions\`
     (or `%APPDATA%\Adobe\CEP\extensions\` for a per-user install)
   - macOS: `/Library/Application Support/Adobe/CEP/extensions/`
     (or `~/Library/Application Support/Adobe/CEP/extensions/`)
2. This is an unsigned/dev extension, so enable debug mode:
   - Windows: add a registry `String` value `PlayerDebugMode` = `1` under
     `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Adobe\CSXS.11` (match the number to your
     CEP version - `.9`/`.10`/`.11`/`.12` all exist; adding it to a couple of
     adjacent numbers doesn't hurt).
   - macOS: `defaults write com.adobe.CSXS.11 PlayerDebugMode 1` (again,
     adjust the number to match).
3. Restart After Effects and/or Premiere Pro. The panel shows up under
   **Window -> Extensions -> Orb Reactor**.

If it doesn't show up, it's almost always the debug-mode key/CSXS version
number mismatch - check `CSXS/manifest.xml`'s `RequiredRuntime Version` against
what `defaults`/registry key you set.

### Host differences

- **After Effects:** PNG sequence (with alpha) and H.264 MP4. Layers are always
  added as new top layers at the CTI (never overwrite existing layers).
- **Premiere Pro:** H.264 MP4 only (PNG sequence is hidden). Clips are placed at
  the playhead (CTI). If video/audio tracks at that time are occupied, the
  plugin picks a free track or adds a new track so existing clips are not cut.

### ffmpeg

Static `ffmpeg` binaries are bundled for both macOS (`bin/mac/ffmpeg`, Intel)
and Windows (`bin/win/ffmpeg.exe`) and auto-detected. On **Apple Silicon** Macs,
a Homebrew install is preferred when present (`brew install ffmpeg`) because the
bundled binary is x86_64 and may require Rosetta. Settings → ffmpeg path shows
what was found and lets you re-detect or override.

## Using it

1. Pick a preset, tweak Shape / Look / Colors to taste. The live preview loops
   continuously so you can judge the motion, not just a still frame.
2. (Optional) Voice Reactivity tab: enable it, load audio, and hit
   **Simulate talking** in the preview header, or just watch it react live
   to your loaded clip as it loops.
3. Export tab: point it at your comp (auto-detected), choose durations/
   resolution/frame rate, pick an output folder, name the layer, and hit
   **Export & place on timeline at CTI**. Move your CTI first if you want it
   somewhere specific - the panel reads it fresh right before importing.

## Troubleshooting

- **Blank/black orb, console shows a shader compile error:** open
  `https://localhost:8090` in Chrome (the `.debug` file in this extension
  wires up that inspector port) and check the console - tell me the exact
  GLSL error and I can patch the specific ported function.
- **"Select a layer... whose source has audio"**: the selected layer's
  `source.hasAudio` came back false - make sure you've actually selected the
  layer (not just scrubbed near it) and that its source file has an audio
  track.
- **Export feels slow on Particle Ribbon**: expected, see above - lower
  `uSegments`/`vSegments` in `renderer.js`, or use a different preset for long
  exports.
## Particles Orb

Added a GPU-instanced Particles Orb style based on the supplied React orb configuration. It exposes particle count, density, size, bloom, orb size, speed, Color From, Color To, and Edge Glow Color controls.
